findings.control_name: DNS A Record Points to Released Elastic IP Address
findings.control_description: Route 53 A record points to an Elastic IP address that has been released. When an Elastic IP is released, it returns to the AWS public IP pool and can be re-allocated by any AWS customer in the same region — including an attacker. The attacker allocates an EC2 instance and associates the reclaimed EIP. The organization's A record now points to the attacker's instance. The attacker can serve any content (phishing, malware, intercepted traffic) on the organization's domain. EIP recycling attacks have been demonstrated by security researchers who successfully reclaimed specific IPs by repeatedly allocating and releasing EIPs in the target region. Complements CTL.ROUTE53.DANGLING.001 (which detects general dangling IPs) by specifically checking whether a Route 53 A record points to a currently-released EIP.

evidence.temporal_risk: Asset non-compliant for 240 hours (SLA: 0 hours). Exposed since 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z.

remediation.description: DNS A record points to an Elastic IP that has been released back to the AWS IP pool and may be re-allocated to an attacker.
remediation.action: If the Elastic IP was released intentionally: remove the Route 53 A record immediately. If the IP was accidentally released: check whether it has been re-allocated by another account via AWS IP address tracking. If the IP is still available, allocate a new EIP and update the Route 53 record. If the IP has been claimed by another account, remove the Route 53 record and allocate a new EIP for a new DNS record.

chain_membership.narrative: Any reclaimable subdomain takeover vector in DNS. An S3 bucket name is reclaimable after deletion (CTL.ROUTE53.DANGLING.S3.001) — attacker creates same-named bucket and serves content; a CloudFront CNAME is unclaimed after distribution deletion (CTL.ROUTE53.DANGLING.CLOUDFRONT.001) — attacker claims the CNAME on their own distribution; an Elastic Beanstalk CNAME is reclaimable after environment termination (CTL.ROUTE53.DANGLING.BEANSTALK.001) — attacker creates an environment with the same CNAME; a released Elastic IP can be reclaimed via pool cycling (CTL.ROUTE53.DANGLING.EIP.001) — attacker's instance receives the organization's traffic; or an NS delegation points to name servers that don't serve the zone (CTL.ROUTE53.DANGLING.NS.001) — attacker who controls the name servers controls all DNS for the subdomain. Threshold of 1 reflects that each independently enables an attacker to serve content or intercept traffic on the organization's domain. Any single reclaimable dangling record is a complete subdomain takeover vector requiring immediate remediation. Linked incidents: Wiz "dangling DNS" campaign analysis (2025, subdomain takeover used for credential phishing in 3 documented APT campaigns), Can I Take Over XYZ project tracking 40+ reclaimable service types across cloud providers.

near_miss_chains.description: Two or more dangling DNS records across different resource types, indicating a systematic DNS cleanup failure rather than an isolated oversight. S3 dangling (CTL.ROUTE53.DANGLING.S3.001), CloudFront dangling (CTL.ROUTE53.DANGLING.CLOUDFRONT.001), ELB dangling (CTL.ROUTE53.DANGLING.ELB.001), EIP dangling (CTL.ROUTE53.DANGLING.EIP.001), EC2 dangling (CTL.ROUTE53.DANGLING.EC2.001), API Gateway dangling (CTL.ROUTE53.DANGLING.APIGATEWAY.001), or Elastic Beanstalk dangling (CTL.ROUTE53.DANGLING.BEANSTALK.001). Threshold of 2 reflects that a single dangling record is an operational failure; two or more across different resource types describes an organization where DNS cleanup is not part of the decommissioning process. Every resource deletion creates a dangling record. The attacker who finds one dangling record in automated scanning will find all of them — the combination amplifies the attack surface. Multiple dangling records indicate that the DNS hygiene problem is systemic, not incidental.
